The Mystery of Consciousness: The You Who Can “Feel”
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well. (Psalm 139:14)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Today I’d like to begin by asking you to do something very simple: look at this line of text on the screen. Good, you’ve seen it. You’ve understood it. And you know that you are looking at it.

Friends, that is actually not simple at all. On the screen there are only some bright and dark points of light, yet you read meaning out of them. Even more amazing, inside you there is an “I” who knows, “I am reading.”

The aroma of your first sip of coffee in the morning, the streak of orange across the evening sky, the ache in your heart when you miss someone far away: all of these are experienced from the “inside.” A doctor can measure your heartbeat, blood pressure and temperature, but no instrument can “feel” for you.

This felt inner world is what we call “consciousness.” Today we are going to walk together into the first gallery of the Mind Hall and look at a mystery that is with us every day, yet that we rarely notice.
The spirit of man is Yahweh’s lamp, searching all his innermost parts. (Proverbs 20:27)
1. Eighty-six billion neurons, and a door we cannot see through
The easy problems and the hard problem

Let me start with a number: the human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons, connected in an extraordinarily complex network. How big is 86 billion? If you counted one per second, you could count until the end of time and still not finish. That little mass on top of your shoulders is really a brilliantly lit megacity.

Scientists are already very skilled. They can measure which regions of your brain are active when you see red or hear a sound. It’s like looking at an office tower at night: you can see clearly which floors have the lights on and which are dark.

But in 1995 the Australian philosopher David Chalmers made a famous distinction. He said that explaining how the brain recognizes and integrates information and controls behavior is the set of “easy problems.” Of course, he admitted they are not easy at all; scientists will be busy with them for generations.

The truly “hard problem” is this: why are these physical processes accompanied by subjective experience? Why, after electrical currents and chemicals rush around, does an “I feel pain” or an “I find this beautiful” appear?
Let’s take an everyday example. A thermometer can measure exactly 38 degrees Celsius, but it does not “feel hot.” It never says, “Ugh, it’s so muggy today, I want the air conditioning on.”
A camera can photograph a rose in perfect detail, every vein of every petal crystal clear, but the camera does not “find it beautiful,” and the rose doesn’t remind it of its first love.
Here lies the mystery of consciousness. Processing information is one thing; “having feelings” is another. Between them stands a door, a door we still cannot see through today.

That is why Proverbs says, “The spirit of man is Yahweh’s lamp, searching all his innermost parts.” There is a lamp inside each of us, lighting up the inner rooms. Instruments can measure the temperature of the bulb, but they cannot explain why the light can “see.”
What this means for us spiritually
Brothers and sisters, this reminds us of something: you are not just the sum of a pile of parts. You are not a walking thermometer, nor a camera that eats meals.
God has lit a lamp inside you. That lamp lets you feel, lets you reflect, lets you ask yourself in the quiet of the night, “Is this the right way to live?” What a noble thing that is!
2. What is it like to be a bat?
Seen from the outside, never fully seen
As early as 1974 the American philosopher Thomas Nagel asked a question that sounds a little funny: “What is it like to be a bat?”

Think about it. Bats use echolocation: they send out sounds, listen to the echoes, and know there is a wall or an insect ahead. Scientists can study this mechanism down to the last detail, draw diagrams and write papers about it.
But even if we understood bat echolocation one hundred percent, we still would not know what it feels like from the inside. Is it like “hearing a picture”? Or something else? We cannot say.

What Nagel wanted to show is that subjective experience seems impossible to exhaust with third-person descriptions alone. It’s like knowing a recipe by heart: you remember the ingredients, the heat and every step, but if you’ve never tasted the dish, you simply don’t know what it tastes like.
Have scientists been trying? Very hard. Science has proposed several theories of consciousness. In 2025 the journal Nature published a large study called an “adversarial collaboration.”

How did the “adversarial” part work? Take the two leading theories: one is called Global Neuronal Workspace Theory, the other Integrated Information Theory. Supporters of each camp first registered their predictions, in black and white, with no changing their story afterwards. Then the predictions were tested with fMRI, MEG and intracranial electrodes in a total of 256 participants.

And the result? Key predictions of both theories failed to find support. It’s a bit like two famous detectives each writing down who the culprit is; when the envelopes are opened, each was only partly right.
Friends, this is not failure; this is honest progress. It tells us that consciousness is still, today, a frontier of science.

Of course, in fairness, there are different views about what consciousness is. There is the physicalist view: Daniel Dennett and others hold that consciousness is entirely brain activity, and that future neuroscience will eventually explain it. There is also realism about the mind, which holds that subjective experience is a real, irreplaceable dimension that physical description cannot fully capture. We respect every friend who thinks seriously about these questions.
For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man, which is in him? Even so, no one knows the things of God, except God’s Spirit. (1 Corinthians 2:11)
What this means for us spiritually
You see, two thousand years ago Paul already said, “For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man, which is in him?” Inside each person is a world no one else can see.
However well your spouse knows you, they cannot hurt for you; however close your best friend is, they cannot shed that tear for you. That deepest room is known only to your own spirit, and to God.
That is not the bad news of loneliness; it is good news. Because the God who knows your deepest places has not left you. He sees, he understands, and he still loves you.
3. Dust plus the breath of life: the mind is a gift
Let’s return to the habit of checking the evidence, and separate what is certain from what is inferred.

What is certain: the human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons; states of consciousness, such as waking, sleep and anesthesia, are closely tied to brain activity; and brain damage changes a person’s conscious experience. So we take care of our brains and we thank God for medicine. All of that is good.
What is still being explored: there is currently no agreed theory of how the brain produces subjective experience.

So what is the inference? Subjective experience is very hard to reduce entirely to the workings of matter. That makes the view that “the mind is real” worth taking seriously. And a personal Creator who is himself spirit naturally explains why conscious minds appear in the universe.

Interestingly, even Nagel, himself an atheist, argued in 2012 that the materialist account is “almost certainly false.” We don’t say “science has proved God,” but all of this reasonably points to this: the source of the mind may well be the God who is himself spirit.
Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul. (Genesis 2:7)

The Bible tells us that human beings come from two sources. One is the dust of the ground, so we have bodies that get tired, grow old and get sick. The other is the breath of life that God breathed in, so man became “a living soul.”
Some say that humans are only dust. That is only half right. Dust shaped by hand makes a very fine clay figure; but God breathed into it, and the figure opened its eyes and said, “Here I am.”
That you can feel, reflect and know that “I” exist is itself a gift. You did not switch on your own light; God did.
What this means for us spiritually

That is why the psalmist says, “I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” Friends, the next time you smell coffee, see a sunset, or are moved by a hymn, don’t just say, “That feels nice.” You can also quietly say, “Lord, thank you for letting me feel.”
The Holy Spirit is my guide

The spirit of man is the Lord’s lamp. A lamp needs power to shine; for our hearts to see clearly, we need the Holy Spirit’s light. I encourage everyone to be still for a moment each day, perhaps just five minutes, and let the Holy Spirit shine into every corner of your heart, to see whether there is any dust, anything hidden away.

We cannot even fully explain our own consciousness; we cannot even explain why we “feel” at all. That alone is enough to humble us. Admit that we are limited, and let God be God. Proud people think they see through everything; humble people know they need the Lord who truly sees through everything.

Since every person has an unseen inner world, then your coworkers, your family, and the brothers and sisters in your fellowship are not tools for getting your work done. Every one of them has a lamp that God has lit.

This week’s action is simple: find a family member or friend and, without rushing to give advice, listen closely for ten minutes as they share what they are feeling. You will find that ten minutes of listening can sometimes be more powerful than an hour of preaching.

Brothers and sisters, science tells us the brain has 86 billion neurons, and that is amazing. Science also honestly tells us that “why there is feeling at all” is still a mystery. And the Bible tells us that the you who can feel, think and know God was made by God’s own hand and given life by his own breath.
Now, let’s all be still for one minute and notice that you are “aware”: your breathing, the sounds around you, the thoughts in your heart. The you who is aware was made by God’s own hand.
And ask yourself: Do I treat myself as nothing more than a machine that works, forgetting that I have a soul that needs God?

Let us pray together: Lord who made me, thank you for giving me a mind that can feel, think and know you. Let your lamp shine into every corner of my inner life, and turn my heart wholly toward you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2. Genesis 2:7 says that human beings are dust plus the breath of God. Do you more easily see yourself as “a machine that works” or as “a living soul”? How does that shape the way you live day to day?

Can We Trust Reason? A Map on Paper and the Real Mountains and Rivers
The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge, but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction. (Proverbs 1:7)
Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Let me start with a little scene. A friend declares with great flair, “I don’t trust any reasoning.” Everyone thinks, “What a free spirit.”

But notice: what is he doing as he says this? He is reasoning. The logic in his head probably goes, “Reasoning often goes wrong, so I don’t trust reasoning.” You see, that itself is a piece of reasoning.
It’s like a man sitting on a chair loudly announcing, “Chairs do not exist!” Friends, he had better stand up before he says that. Even to doubt reason, you must first trust reason.

We use reason every day: balancing accounts, planning schedules, understanding a paragraph, judging whether a news story is believable. But today I want us to stop and ask a question we rarely ask: why should reason itself be trusted?
The universe can actually be understood

In 1936 Einstein wrote that one may say the eternal mystery of the world is its comprehensibility. That line was later popularly passed around as “The most incomprehensible thing about the universe is that it is comprehensible.” That is a paraphrase, but the meaning is close.

Think about it: the universe could have been a tangled mess with no regularity at all, apples falling down today and flying up tomorrow. But it isn’t. It has order, and that order can be understood by people.

There are two “just so” facts here. First, the human mind can grasp logic and mathematics. Second, the universe actually runs according to mathematics. The two just happen to fit together, like a key that slides perfectly into a lock.

In 1960 the Nobel Prize–winning physicist Eugene Wigner called this phenomenon “the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences.” He also said it is “a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve.” That a great scientist would use the word “gift” is well worth savoring.

Let’s use an analogy. Imagine you are shut in a room with no windows, only paper and a pencil. Working purely from reasoning, you draw a map. Then you open the door, step outside, and look: there is the mountain, there is the river, matching your map at every point. Wouldn’t you be startled?
That is often how it goes with the structures mathematicians work out on paper: only later is it discovered that they describe nature exactly.

Here is a real example. In 1928 Paul Dirac wrote down an equation describing the electron. Its solutions implied that there should exist a positively charged “anti-electron.” At the time no one had ever seen such a thing.
Then in 1932 Carl Anderson actually found the positron in cosmic rays. First drawn on paper, later found in the sky. Isn’t that exactly the “map on paper”?
The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge, but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction. (Proverbs 1:7)
What this means for us spiritually

Proverbs says the fear of the Lord is the “beginning” of knowledge. Beginning means starting point, foundation. When someone acknowledges that there is a wise God behind the universe and then studies the universe, it is like reading a book that has an author: the more you read, the richer it gets, because you know there is meaning in it to be found.
Reason is not the enemy of faith; it is God’s gift for knowing the truth.

I love this picture: a little child is watching ants through a magnifying glass, completely absorbed, and then looks up and asks, “Daddy, why do ants walk in a line?” That “why” is the spark of curiosity God has placed in the human heart.

The church doesn’t need to fear that spark. A child who asks questions doesn’t have small faith; he is using the gift God gave him. Our job is to look for answers alongside him, and to let him know that God is the source of all truth.
2. C. S. Lewis’s argument from reason, and a gracious admission of error
If thought is only the product of non-rational causes

In his book Miracles, C. S. Lewis put forward an “argument from reason.” His point was roughly this: if our thoughts are entirely the product of non-rational causes, then we have little reason to believe they are true.

Here’s a comparison. If a calculator had been thrown together at random, with no one designing it to get the right answer, and its screen showed “one plus one equals two,” would you fully trust it? Maybe it happened to be right, but you’d never feel quite sure.
After the flaws were pointed out

The best part of the story comes next. In 1948 the philosopher Elizabeth Anscombe pointed out flaws in Lewis’s argument. Friends, Lewis was already very famous by then. If someone had picked holes in our work to our face, we might have lost face, gone home and written a long rebuttal.
But what did Lewis do? He humbly accepted the criticism, and in the revised 1960 edition he rewrote Chapter 3.
That itself is a fine example of intellectual honesty. People who truly believe in truth are not afraid of being corrected, because what they love is the truth, not their own reputation.
You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free. (John 8:32)
What this means for us spiritually
The Lord Jesus said the truth will make us free. Being corrected by the truth is not humiliation; it is release.

Brothers and sisters, at church, at home and at work, we often hold our ground just to save face. Yet “I was wrong” may be the most freeing sentence there is. By rewriting a whole chapter, Lewis shows us that faith and intellectual honesty can walk hand in hand.
3. Where does the real conflict lie?
The contemporary philosopher Alvin Plantinga proposed an argument with a very long name: the “evolutionary argument against naturalism.” Don’t let the name scare you; let’s take it slowly.

He said that natural selection favors behavior that helps survival, not necessarily beliefs that are true. If “naturalism,” the view that there is no God, and evolution are both true, then the probability that our cognitive faculties are reliable is low, or simply impossible to assess.
In that case the naturalist loses any guarantee even for his own reasoning. It’s a bit like sawing off the branch you are sitting on.

Let me put it in more everyday terms. Suppose there is a bathroom scale by your door, and all you know is that it was designed “to put you in a good mood,” not “to tell you your real weight.” Would you still trust the number it shows every day? It might keep telling you, “You’ve lost weight!” You’d be delighted, but it might not be true.
Plantinga’s point is this: if our brains were selected only to “stay alive,” not designed to “see the truth,” then it is hard to be sure that the answers they give us are true.
So Plantinga’s conclusion is that the real conflict is not between science and faith, but between science and naturalism.

We also need to be fair. Philosophers such as Fitelson and Sober argue that Plantinga’s probability reasoning is flawed; others argue that true beliefs usually aid survival, so evolution is enough to explain why reason is broadly reliable.

The theist response is this: even if true beliefs often aid survival, this still assumes a world with a stable, intelligible order. Theism holds that mind and universe come from the same wise God, so their fit is no coincidence.

Let’s check what is certain and what is inferred. What is certain: mathematics has astonishing predictive power in physics; the Dirac equation predicted the positron, which was discovered later. What is still debated: natural selection preserves abilities that aid survival, but scholars still debate how “aiding survival” relates to “seeing the truth.” And the reliability of reason and the intelligibility of the universe both point to a rational Creator; that is a philosophical inference, and we do not call it a scientific proof.
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them. (Genesis 1:27)
Many early scientists believed the universe has order because the God who made it is faithful, and that humans can understand the universe because they are made in God’s image.

It’s like a key and a lock made by the same locksmith: of course they fit. Your mind and this universe come from the same wise God. Every time you think, every time something finally clicks, you are using his gift.

Reason is a good tool, but a tool needs a guideline. However sharp a carpenter’s saw, without a chalk line it will cut crooked. God’s Word is that chalk line. Let our thinking happen in the light of Scripture: not switching off our brains, but pointing them in the right direction.
Changing our mindset changes our lives

Much of the time our knowledge of God stays at the level of “information”: we have heard it, we know it, we can recite it. But moving from “information” to “revelation” takes the work of the Holy Spirit. Ask the Holy Spirit to turn the knowledge in our heads into conviction in our hearts, changing from a human point of view to God’s point of view.

The more we learn about the universe, the more we admit our limits. Wigner called the effectiveness of mathematics a gift “we neither understand nor deserve,” and those words themselves carry humility. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge, and humility is the starting point of wisdom.

This week’s action: choose one question about faith you have had recently, write it down, study a related Bible passage, and talk it through with a spiritual companion. Don’t be afraid of questions; God is not afraid of your questions.

Brothers and sisters, today we have seen that the universe can be understood and that humans can understand it. Together these two “just so” facts reasonably point to a God who gave us reason and made the universe with a rational order.
Think of what you have used reason for today: balancing accounts, making plans, understanding a paragraph. Every act of thinking is using a gift from God.
And honestly ask yourself: Do I use reason to seek the truth, or to find excuses for what I already want to do?
Let us pray together: God of wisdom, thank you for giving me a mind that can think. Renew my mind, so that my reason bows to your truth and is lit by your Word. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2. When his mistake was pointed out, C. S. Lewis rewrote an entire chapter. How do you usually react when someone corrects you? How can we, like him, “love truth more than saving face”?
3. Do you currently have an unresolved question about faith? Would you be willing to share it with your small group and plan to study the Scriptures on it together?
The Moral Law Written on the Heart: That Cry of “Not Fair!”
He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God? (Micah 6:8)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Any family with children knows this scene: there’s one piece of cake on the table and two children to share it. The older brother cuts it and immediately takes the bigger piece for himself. Before he can say a word, the younger one is already shouting, “That’s not fair!”
Friends, who taught that little one the definition of “fair”? No one. He has never taken an ethics class or read a law book, but he simply knows that a line has been crossed.

C. S. Lewis noticed something very interesting too. When people quarrel, they rarely say, “I’m stronger than you, so do what I say.” Instead they say, “You shouldn’t do that,” “You promised,” “How would you like it if someone did that to you?”

Have you noticed? Both sides of a quarrel are quietly appealing to the same standard. Without that standard there could be no real quarrel at all, only a contest of whose fist is bigger. Today we’re going to look at where that standard comes from.

In 2019 a research team at the University of Oxford analyzed ethnographic records from 60 societies. They wanted to know: do people around the world actually share any common views about what is “good”?

They found seven cooperative behaviors that were regarded as good in the societies studied. Let me read them to you: helping family, helping your group, returning favors, courage, deference to superiors, dividing resources fairly, and respecting others’ property.

Even more interesting, they found no society that regarded these behaviors as bad. The differences between cultures were only in how they ranked them: some put more weight on family, some more on the group.
Of course, the researchers honestly note that more detailed tests with new data are still needed. We won’t exaggerate, but this finding is certainly worth stopping to think about.

Let’s use music as a comparison. The world’s musical styles vary endlessly: Chinese traditional music, jazz, rock, hymns. They sound worlds apart, but underneath they are all built on a few shared intervals and rhythms.
Morality is like that: each culture plays a different tune, but beneath them lies the same “scale.”

Travel to any country and you may not understand a word of the language, but if you see someone risk their life to save a child who has fallen into the water, you don’t need a translator to know that is good. If you see someone snatch an old woman’s purse, you don’t need a translator either; you know that is wrong. That is the shared “scale.”

For when Gentiles who don’t have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves, in that they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience testifying with them, and their thoughts among themselves accusing or else excusing them. (Romans 2:14–15)
What this means for us spiritually
Paul said it long ago: even people without the law have a conscience bearing witness within them. The work of the law is “written in their hearts.”

This standard was not invented by humans; it was engraved by the God who made us. Just as a craftsman carves his mark on the underside of his work, God has engraved the mark of his righteousness on the tablet of every human heart.
2. Not just instinct, and not just custom
Some say morality is nothing more than instinct. In Book One of Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis responds that it isn’t that simple.

Imagine you’re walking by a river and hear someone who has fallen in crying for help. One instinct in you wants to help. At the same time another instinct wants to protect yourself: the current is so strong, I could die too. The two instincts are fighting.

At that moment there is a third voice inside you, telling you which one you “ought” to follow. That third voice is not itself an instinct. It’s like the keys on a piano: some are high and some are low, but what tells you which key to play now is the sheet music, not the keys.

Others say morality is just social custom. But Lewis points out that we say one society’s morality is better than another’s. For example, we say a society that abolished slavery is better than a society that traded in slaves.
If morality were only custom, there would only be “different,” never “better.” The fact that we can say “better” means there is a standard higher than every society.

At this point I’d like to share an example of honesty with you. In 2007 an experiment reported that infants aged 6 to 10 months preferred a “helper” puppet over a “hinderer” puppet. Many people were thrilled when they heard it: look, babies are born with a moral sense!
But in 2025 a large replication across 37 laboratories with 567 infants did not reproduce this preference.

So we should not present a single study as settled fact. Brothers and sisters, our faith does not need exaggerated evidence to prop it up. Truth is not afraid of being tested, and we don’t need to pick out only what suits us.

It’s like a witness in court. A good witness won’t claim to have seen what he didn’t see just to help a friend. Christian witness is the same: say what is certain is certain, and say what is still debated is still debated. That kind of witness is what others can trust.

Where do moral intuitions come from? There is the evolutionary explanation, which says moral intuitions may be products of evolution that promote cooperation; the philosopher Sharon Street even argues that, if so, we have little reason to believe our moral intuitions reflect objective moral truth.

The moral argument responds: evolution can explain “how” we came to have a moral sense, but not that “harming the innocent really is wrong.” If morality is only a survival strategy, that statement loses its real weight, and most people cannot accept that conclusion.
So C. S. Lewis’s famous moral argument says: if there is a universal, objective moral law binding on everyone, the best explanation is a good Lawgiver. It is an inference, but a weighty one.
He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God? (Micah 6:8)
What this means for us spiritually

The prophet Micah says, “He has shown you, O man, what is good.” God has not left us groping in the dark. He engraved the standard on our hearts and made it clear in his Word: act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God.
3. Knowing the good is not the same as doing it
At this point we might feel rather pleased with ourselves: that’s right, I have a standard in my heart; I know what is right.

But brothers and sisters, think honestly: is knowing what is good the same as doing it? Every one of us has gone against the standard in our own hearts. When we measure others, the ruler is very precise; when it comes to measuring ourselves, the ruler suddenly seems to stretch.
It’s like someone who stands by a scale weighing everyone else every day, announcing who has gained and who has lost, but never daring to step on it himself.
The standard points to a Lawgiver, and to a Savior
So this standard points not only to a Lawgiver; it also shows us that we need salvation. A ruler can tell you how crooked you are, but it cannot straighten you out.

It’s like a mirror. You look in the mirror in the morning and see a smudge on your face; the mirror faithfully tells you, “You’re dirty.” But you wouldn’t wipe your face with the mirror, would you? The mirror’s job is to show you the problem; to wash your face you need water. Conscience is that mirror, and what can wash us clean is God’s grace.
That is exactly the good news of the gospel.
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. (John 3:16)
The righteous God who engraved his law on our hearts is also the loving God who sent his Son to save us. He doesn’t just hand us a ruler; he came himself to lift up those of us who don’t measure up.

Conscience is precious, but conscience also needs calibrating. Like a watch that runs slow after a while, it needs to be reset often. Let the Bible be my final standard of right and wrong, not my feelings, and not “everyone else is doing it.”

Morality is not just rules; it is living out the fruit of the Spirit in relationships: goodness, faithfulness, gentleness. (920 is our shorthand for living out the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.) Someone who can recite the rules but is harsh with their family has not yet truly understood God’s law.
Measure yourself with this standard first, then others. Once we have honestly measured ourselves, our hands will be a little gentler when we measure others.
This week’s action: each evening this week, take three minutes to review the day: was there something I knew I should do but didn’t? Confess it to God and make it right the next day.

Brothers and sisters, that cry of “Not fair!” is not just a child being willful; it reveals a standard within the human heart. Cultures everywhere share a common scale, and conscience bears witness within us. All of this reasonably points to a good Lawgiver.
Recall a moment when seeing injustice made your heart burn. That righteous anger reflects God’s righteous character.
And quietly ask yourself: I measure others strictly by the standard in my heart. Am I just as honest when I measure myself?

Let us pray together: Righteous and good God, thank you for writing your law on my heart. Forgive me where I have knowingly done wrong, and give me strength to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2. The infant study was not reproduced, and the speaker reminded us not to present a single study as settled fact. What attitude do you think Christians should take when citing science?
3. Micah 6:8 speaks of acting justly, loving mercy and walking humbly. Of these three, which do you most need to practice this week?
Free Will and Responsibility: A Robot’s “I Love You”
Choose today whom you will serve … but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh. (Joshua 24:15)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Imagine a brilliant engineer who designs a robot for his wife. Every morning at exactly seven o’clock, the robot walks up to her and says in a very tender voice, “Darling, I love you.”
One day, two days, three hundred sixty-five days, rain or shine, never late. Tell me, would his wife be moved?

The first day she might find it novel; by the third day it would probably feel a bit creepy. Why? Because the robot cannot choose “not to say it.” Its “I love you” is essentially no different from a rice cooker announcing, “The rice is ready.”

Love is precious precisely because it could be withheld, yet is freely given. When God made human beings, he gave them this ability to choose. Today we’re going to talk about a topic that is very deep, yet one we bump into every day: free will and responsibility.

In 1983 the neuroscientist Benjamin Libet carried out a famous experiment. He asked participants to flex their wrist whenever they felt like it, while watching a clock and noting where the hand was at the moment they “decided to move.”
He found that brain activity called the “readiness potential” began several hundred milliseconds before the moment participants were aware of deciding.
That caused quite a stir. Many people concluded: you see, the brain had already decided, and you only “felt” like you were deciding afterwards. Free will is just an illusion!

Let’s look at it first through an analogy. A ship at sea is constantly pushed by wind and waves. That is real; no one can deny it. Yet the helmsman is still at the wheel, deciding where the ship goes.
The brain’s mechanisms are like the wind and waves: they are real, but they do not necessarily replace the one at the helm. Feeling the wind and waves does not mean there is no helmsman on board.

I call heaven and earth to witness against you today that I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your descendants. (Deuteronomy 30:19)
What this means for us spiritually

From beginning to end, the Bible treats people as those who can choose. Moses says, “I have set before you life and death … therefore choose life.” If people could not choose at all, those words would be like telling a washing machine, “Please choose whether you want to do the laundry today.” It would be meaningless.
God tells you to “choose life” because he has truly placed the helm in your hands. That is respect, and it is also responsibility.

Sometimes we really want to hand the helm over and say, “Lord, just decide for me.” But God is like a good father: he walks with you, teaches you and reminds you, but he will not turn you into a remote-control car. He wants you to grow up and learn to choose him for yourself.

In fact, Libet himself did not think this was the end of free will. He believed that consciousness can still “veto” the impulse before the action. It’s like reaching for a third piece of cake: your hand is already out, a voice inside says, “No, self-control,” and you pull your hand back.

Then in 2012 Aaron Schurger and colleagues proposed a model: the readiness potential may simply be a build-up of the brain’s spontaneous fluctuations, triggering the action only when it crosses a threshold, and it does not mean that “the decision was already made.”

It’s a bit like waves at the seashore, rising and falling one after another, and once in a while one rises higher than the seawall. You can’t look at the rising waves and say, “The seawall had already decided to get wet.”

Please remember that these are very fine-grained studies, and scientists are still debating them. We don’t need to rush to say “science has proved free will,” and we don’t need to be frightened by headlines saying “science has proved there is no free will.” The honest thing to say is that the subject is far more complicated than the headlines.
Flexing a wrist is not the same as forgiving someone
There’s another important point. Experiments like this study movements such as “flick your hand whenever you like,” actions with no reason and no consequences.

But the truly important choices in life, such as: Will I forgive the person who hurt me? Will I keep my marriage covenant? Will I report my expenses honestly? These often involve long reflection, prayer and struggle. The two are very different.
Using “flexing a wrist” to conclude “you cannot choose whether to love” is like using “picking a piece of candy” to explain “how you choose a lifelong partner.” It’s far too big a leap.

I think of the testimonies of many brothers and sisters. Some have kept watch by a hospital bed for three years, and every morning when they wake up they must choose again: Will I keep loving today? Will I keep caring? Choices like that are written with tears, prayers and persistence day after day; they can never be explained by a few hundred milliseconds of electrical potential.
Checking the evidence, and different views

Let’s sort things out. What is certain: before spontaneous movements, a readiness potential can be measured in the brain, and it appears before participants are aware of deciding. What is still debated: whether the readiness potential represents a “decision” or a “build-up of random fluctuations” is still being discussed in neuroscience.

In philosophy and theology there are also different views. Determinism holds that every choice is determined by prior causes and that freedom is only a feeling; critics point out that this makes it hard to ground moral responsibility. Compatibilism holds that as long as an action comes from your own will and is not forced by outside pressure, it is free, and that freedom and causation can coexist; many Reformed theologians hold a similar view. Libertarian free will holds that in the very same situation a person truly could have chosen otherwise; many theologians in the Arminian tradition hold this view.

Evangelicals differ on this question, and this is an area where we can be gracious with one another. But all affirm one thing: people are accountable to God for their choices. Unity on the core, charity on the edges.
For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another. (Galatians 5:13)
What this means for us spiritually
Paul says we were called to freedom. But freedom is not a license for indulgence; it is the starting line of love. Freedom at its most beautiful looks like “through love be servants to one another.”
3. Love needs freedom; freedom is for love
If people had no choice at all
Let’s think about it: what if people had no choice at all?

First, moral responsibility would be meaningless. A judge could not find anyone guilty, because “his brain did it, not him.” Second, genuine love would be meaningless, like the robot that says “I love you” at seven every morning. Third, even rational thought would be meaningless, because your conclusions would not be reached by you; they would simply be pushed out of you.
So real human choice fits the teaching that humans are made in God’s image. That is a philosophical and theological inference.
Why would God take this risk?
C. S. Lewis argued that by giving humans free will God made evil possible, but also made possible a love worth having.

Friends, God could have made a world where no one could go wrong and no one could love, like a room full of neatly lined-up robots. Instead he chose to make a world where people can say “no.” Why? Because he wanted children, not machines.

Parents understand this best. When your child is little, you pick him up and he has no say in it. But when he grows up and goes out into the world, and one day calls home on his own and says, “Mom, Dad, I miss you,” that one phone call moves you more than a thousand hugs from his childhood. Because he chose it himself.
We love him, because he first loved us. (1 John 4:19)
What this means for us spiritually
Our love is a response to God’s loving us first. God loved first, placed freedom in our hands, and then waits. He waits for us to say, like Joshua, “As for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.”

What is the best use of freedom? To freely hand the throne to Jesus. It sounds like a contradiction, but it isn’t. A pianist is most free not when banging random keys, but when submitting to the music and playing with complete abandon. When we let Jesus reign, we live in true freedom.

True freedom is not doing whatever you want; it is being “able” to choose love and service, living the self-emptied life in Christ. Someone bound by their temper, their desires or their phone may look like they can do anything, but they are the least free of all.

Since choice is real, responsibility is real too. Take responsibility for your choices; when you are wrong, admit it, correct course and start again. Don’t blame everything on your genes, your circumstances or the family you grew up in. These all have an influence, like the wind and waves; but the helm is still in your hands.
This week’s action: pick one thing you have always blamed on other people or your circumstances, write down “one choice I can make,” and act on it this week.

Brothers and sisters, science tells us the brain’s readiness potential is real, but what it means is still debated. The Bible tells us that God sets choices before us because what he wants is real love.
Think about it: what choice today could you use to express love for God and for others?
And honestly ask yourself: Do I often blame my choices on circumstances, genes or other people, unwilling to take responsibility?

Let us pray together: Lord Jesus, thank you for giving me the freedom to choose. Today I choose once again to let you reign. May my freedom not become an excuse for indulgence, but a way to serve others in love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2. In the analogy of the wind, the waves and the helmsman, what are the “wind and waves” in your life? Under those influences, what choices can you still make?
3. Is there something you have always blamed on other people or your circumstances? What is the “one choice” you are willing to make this week?
Longing for Eternity: Homesick for a Home We Have Never Seen

He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end. (Ecclesiastes 3:11)
Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Think back: what was the one thing you wanted most as a child? Maybe a bicycle, a box of colored pens, a doll.
You waited for it for so long, and the day you finally got it, you were too excited to sleep. But a week later? It sat in a corner gathering dust, and you started wanting the next thing.
Friends, doesn’t that sound familiar? Our hearts are like a cup with a hole in it: however much you pour in, before long it’s empty again.

It’s the same when we grow up, only the things get more expensive: a new phone, a new car, a promotion, a raise, a bigger house. You finally get the thing you hoped for so long, yet the happiness quickly fades.

But there is another kind of experience. One night you look up at a sky full of stars, or hear a moving hymn, and suddenly an inexpressible longing wells up in your heart, as if you were homesick for a home, a home you have never been to.

More than sixteen hundred years ago, Augustine opened his Confessions by saying something to God that, in essence, runs: you made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. Today let’s talk about that “restlessness.”
1. We want not only to live, but to know why we live
Three longings of the human heart

There are at least three deep longings in our hearts. The first is meaning: people want not only to live, but to know why they live. The second is beauty: beautiful scenery, music and art move us, yet always leave a longing that says “this isn’t enough.” The third is justice: when we see injustice, we long for the day when everything is set right.
Let’s start with the first: meaning.
The psychiatrist Viktor Frankl was imprisoned in Nazi concentration camps. He survived, and later wrote a book called Man’s Search for Meaning; the German original was published in 1946.
In the book he records an observation: in the worst conditions, those who could find a meaning to live for were often better able to endure.
Think about it: the same hunger, the same cold, the same despair; some collapsed and some came through. The difference was not only in their bodies, but in whether they had a “why” in their hearts.
This reminds us that what people fear most may not be hardship, but hardship without meaning. When your heart has a “why,” even a heavy burden becomes easier to carry.
Frankl later developed “logotherapy,” whose core claim is that the search for meaning affects a person’s ability to face suffering. It also inspired later research in the psychology of meaning.
It’s like a phone battery. A battery doesn’t just switch the phone on; it’s what keeps the phone going all day. Meaning is the battery of the human heart.

We know people like this too. There is an elderly man with many aches and illnesses, yet every time you see him he is beaming. Ask him how he keeps going, and he says, “Every day I pray for my grandchildren. That’s my job, and the Lord hasn’t told me to clock out yet.” Friends, that is the power of meaning.
You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more. (Psalm 16:11)
What this means for us spiritually
The psalmist says God “will show me the path of life.” Our deepest meaning is not something we invent ourselves; it is received from the One who made us.
Only in his presence is there “fullness” of joy. Notice that word: fullness. The joys of this world are often “almost, but not quite”; only in God’s presence is there fullness.

We can ask ourselves: what made me happiest today? How long will that happiness last? If the answer is “it’ll be gone by tonight,” then perhaps we have been drinking water that keeps leaking away, and have not yet come to the eternal spring.
2. Babies get hungry because food exists
C. S. Lewis’s argument from desire
C. S. Lewis has a beautiful argument called the “argument from desire.” Let’s explain it with a comparison.
Babies get hungry because food exists; people get thirsty because water exists; people get sleepy because there is such a thing as sleep. Every natural desire has a corresponding satisfaction.
So if the human heart has a longing that nothing in this world can satisfy, what does that tell us? Perhaps it shows that we were made for another world.
In Mere Christianity, Lewis wrote, in essence, that if I find in myself a desire that no experience in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that I was made for another world.
What about people who want to fly?
Of course, someone will object: wanting something doesn’t mean it exists! People want to fly; does that mean people can fly?

That’s a good question. Lewis made a distinction. One kind is “natural desire,” such as hunger and sleep: everyone has them, and they all have corresponding satisfactions. The other kind is “fanciful desire,” such as wanting to fly or wanting to visit fairyland: not everyone has them, and they aren’t necessary for life.
He argued that the longing for eternity belongs to the first kind: it is universal, and nothing in all creation satisfies it.

We must also say honestly that this is a philosophical inference, not a strict proof. Naturalist friends will say this longing may be a by-product of evolution or psychology, a wish that humans project outward. Theism holds that a longing that is universal, deep and never satisfied in this world looks more like something pointing to its true object.

It’s like a key. You find a beautifully made key on the road, but it won’t open any door you’ve tried in the whole world. Would you say, “This key is useless,” or would you think, “There must be a door that it was made for”?

Some people carry this key all their lives, trying achievement, money, romance and fame. Every door seems to open a crack, but none ever truly opens. Brothers and sisters, it’s not that the key is broken; it was made from the start for the door that is God.

He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end. (Ecclesiastes 3:11)
What this means for us spiritually
Ecclesiastes says God “has also set eternity in their hearts.” The Hebrew word here means “forever.” God has placed a longing for eternity in every human heart.
Why? So that we would not be content with temporary things, but would come and seek him. That “restlessness” is not a malfunction but a design; not a punishment but an invitation.

It’s like migratory birds. As soon as autumn comes, something stirs inside them and they want to fly south; even a bird in a cage will beat its wings. That stirring is not a defect; it is the sense of direction the Creator placed within them. The stirring for eternity in the human heart is just the same.
3. The signpost is not the destination
Beauty and justice point the way too

Now the other two longings. Beauty: you stand on a mountaintop watching the sunrise, so beautiful it takes your breath away, yet the longer you look, the more it feels as if there is a greater beauty behind it, and this sunrise is only its shadow.
Justice: you watch the news and see innocent people oppressed, and you think, surely one day this will be set right? Yet the courts and systems of this world have never fully set things right.

These longings are like signposts. Signposts are important, but they are not the destination. If you were driving on a trip and saw a sign saying “To the Beach,” and then pitched your tent under the sign, had a barbecue, took selfies and said, “We’ve arrived,” that would be a real shame.

In our lives we often pitch our tents under the signposts. We treat a good job as the destination, a happy family as the destination, even the fruit of our ministry as the destination. These are all good things, but their value lies in pointing to the One who is further on.
while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal. (2 Corinthians 4:18)
What this means for us spiritually

Paul says the things which are seen are temporal, and the things which are not seen are eternal. The good things of this world are real gifts, and we can enjoy them with thanksgiving; but don’t mistake the gift for the Giver.
The psalmist Asaph spoke the deepest confession of the human heart:
Who do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth who I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever. (Psalm 73:25–26)
Our bodies grow old and our hearts fail, but God is our portion forever. That is the “home we have never been to, yet always long for.”
From the temporary to the eternal

Measure today’s time, money and energy with eternity in view. One simple question can help us: a hundred years from now, will this still matter? Many things that keep you awake with worry today will be remembered by no one in a hundred years; but praying for someone, or leading someone to know the Lord, will still be shining in heaven a hundred years from now.
Let Jesus receive all the glory

Every good thing is a signpost pointing to him; don’t mistake the signpost for the destination. When we enjoy good food, beautiful scenery and good relationships, let our thanks return to God, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

For example, a child gets a wonderful birthday present, tears it open, jumps for joy, and runs off to play without so much as a glance at the person who gave it. Wouldn’t the parents feel a little hurt? Sometimes we treat God that way.

Thank God in every beautiful moment, and let enjoyment become worship. After a good meal, say, “Lord, thank you.” When you see a lovely day, say, “Lord, you are beautiful.” That way temporary things become windows onto eternity.

Try this: every night this week before bed, recall one small good thing and say thank you to God. You’ll find that thanksgiving is like a window: the more you open it, the wider it gets, and the more light fills your heart.

This week’s action: list three things you have recently poured the most energy into, and ask yourself: a hundred years from now, which of them will still matter? Adjust one, and give that time to eternal things.

Brothers and sisters, the human heart has a longing that nothing in this world can fill. Frankl saw that people need meaning, C. S. Lewis saw that we were made for another world, and Ecclesiastes tells us that it is God who set eternity in the human heart.
Today the Lord Jesus gives you this invitation too:
Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. (Matthew 11:28)
Recall a beautiful moment that made you think, “I want more.” Bring that longing before God and acknowledge that only he can satisfy it.
And ask yourself: What have I recently tried to use to fill the emptiness in my heart?

Let us pray together: Eternal God, you have set eternity in my heart. Forgive me for seeking satisfaction from temporary things. Let me find fullness of joy in your presence, and fix my eyes on the eternal things that cannot be seen. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. Have you ever “waited a long time for something, only to find the happiness quickly faded once you had it”? What does that experience tell you the human heart needs?
2. Thinking about the analogy “the signpost is not the destination,” is there a good thing in your life that you have, without realizing it, treated as the destination?
3. List three things you have recently poured the most energy into. Which of them will still matter a hundred years from now? How do you plan to adjust?
The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth. (John 1:14)
Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! I’d like you to listen to this sentence: “This morning a penguin wearing a red scarf haggled at the market with the old man who sells tofu pudding.”

All right, you laughed. But notice: you have certainly never heard that sentence before, and quite possibly no one in the world has ever said it in exactly that way. Yet you understood it instantly, and a picture even popped into your head.
What an amazing thing that is! A few dozen sounds and a few thousand words can produce an unlimited number of new sentences. We can talk about the past, the future, things never seen, love and truth.
Through language, the meaning in one heart travels into another. Language is like a bridge connecting two islands that were once separated by the sea. Today let’s take a walk across that bridge.

Think about it: if there were no language in the world, how would you tell your family “I love you”? How would you apologize to a friend? How would you pray to God? Perhaps a look or a hug could express part of it, but the finer feelings of the heart would probably stay stuck inside, unable to get out.
Human language has some very distinctive features.

First, unlimited combinations. A limited set of words plus grammatical rules can build an unlimited number of sentences, nested layer upon layer. For example: “I know you think he said she won’t come.” One sentence inside another, like Russian nesting dolls, layer within layer, and you still understand it.

Second, it can talk about things that aren’t here. The past, the future, abstract justice and hope can all be put into words. We can say “this day next year,” we can say “the kingdom of heaven,” we can say “forgiveness,” none of which are things sitting on the table that you can touch.
Third, everyone can learn it. The world has more than seven thousand languages, and every normally developing child learns the language around them within a few years.

Friends, that third point is astonishing when you think about it. Adults learning a foreign language memorize vocabulary until their heads spin and get the grammar all tangled up; little children, with no classes and no exams, can talk back to you within three or four years, and argue their case quite convincingly.

Even more interesting, children don’t just memorize sentences adults have said; they make up new sentences of their own. Sometimes they’re so creative that the adults burst out laughing. That shows what they have learned is not a set of recordings, one sentence at a time, but a system of rules that can “generate” new sentences.

Language is like LEGO bricks. LEGO comes in only a few dozen shapes, yet you can build houses, castles and spaceships, an endless variety of creations. Language is the same: limited parts, unlimited creativity.
When we talk every day, it’s like building with LEGO every day. The same few bricks can build a warm house, or a tall wall. What gets built often depends on what the builder wants in their heart.

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made. (John 1:1–3)
What this means for us spiritually
John’s Gospel opens by saying, “In the beginning was the Word.” This “Word” is the Greek logos, meaning both word and reason.

The God of the Bible is not a silent God; he is a God who speaks and communicates. He created all things through his word, and through his word he reveals himself to us. We can speak because the God who spoke first made us in his image.
2. The story of Nim the chimpanzee
In the 1970s the psychologist Herbert Terrace carried out an experiment: teaching a chimpanzee sign language. The chimpanzee was called “Nim.”
Nim was very clever and learned many signs. At first everyone was excited: maybe apes could chat with people too!
But when Terrace’s team carefully analyzed the videotapes, they found that most of Nim’s signs imitated his trainers, and he did not produce grammatically structured sentences.

It’s a bit like a parrot that learns to say “Happy New Year!” It says it perfectly, and everyone is delighted at New Year; but ask it, “What are your plans for next year?” and it still says, “Happy New Year!”
Recursion: the ability to nest layer upon layer

In 2002 three scholars, Marc Hauser, Noam Chomsky and Tecumseh Fitch, proposed in the journal Science that “recursion,” the ability to nest structures layer upon layer, may be the uniquely human core of language. That’s the Russian nesting dolls we just mentioned: one sentence can be tucked inside another.

Animals also communicate in rich ways. Honeybees dance to tell their companions where the flowers are, and monkeys give alarm calls to warn one another of danger. These are all marvelous, and worth praising God’s creation for.
But there is currently no evidence that they have this kind of open-ended, infinitely combinable grammar.

This makes us treasure even more the gift God has given us. We may say a great many words in a day without ever stopping to think that being able to speak and to understand others is itself a miracle.

We must also be honest: scholars still debate how the human capacity for language originated and whether recursion is truly its uniquely human core. How language began remains one of the hardest questions in science.

Out of the ground Yahweh God formed every animal of the field, and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. Whatever the man called every living creature became its name. (Genesis 2:19)
What this means for us spiritually
You see, in Genesis God gave Adam the task of naming. It was the first time a human being used language to take part in God’s creation.

Every parent knows that naming a child is a big deal: you look through dictionaries, think about meanings, ask the grandparents, because a name carries blessing and hope. That God entrusted something so important to Adam shows how much he values human words.

God brought the animals to Adam one by one, as if to say, “Come, give this one a name.” Adam said, “This one is called …” and God said, “Good, that’s its name.” Friends, what trust and honor that is! God invites us to join in his work through language.

We can reasonably infer that humans’ ability to express meaning and build relationships through language is best explained by our being made in the image of this speaking God. That is a philosophical and theological inference.
But the Bible tells us something even more wonderful. The Word who created language and made all things through his word did not just speak from heaven.
The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth. (John 1:14)
Friends, it’s as if an author not only wrote a book for you, but walked into the book himself, became one of its characters, sat down beside you and spoke to you in words you could understand.

Knowing an invisible God is so hard for us; but God, in his kindness toward us, became human himself, and came among us in human form, with a human voice and human language. Jesus is the clearest word God has ever spoken to humanity.
So when we read Jesus’ words in the four Gospels, we are really hearing God speak to us in person, in a way we can understand.
His words are “full of grace and truth.” Truth without grace makes words that wound; grace without truth makes words that are empty. Jesus’ words are full of both.

Think of how Jesus spoke to the Samaritan woman, or to Peter. He never pretended sin didn’t exist; that is truth. Yet whenever he spoke, people felt there was a way forward and a home to return to; that is grace.
We are often the exact opposite: polite to outsiders and blunt with our families; easy on ourselves and hard on others. Lord, teach us to speak as you do.
What this means for us spiritually

So language is not just a tool for communication; it is a noble gift God has given us. The same mouth can build people up or tear them down, can bless or curse. Since the Word saved us through words, our words should also carry grace and truth.

God speaks through his Word, and his words are written in the Bible. Reading the Bible every day is hearing God speak every day; let his words gradually become my words. What comes out of a person’s mouth is often what fills their heart. When your heart is full of God’s Word, grace naturally flows from your lips.

You can think of Bible reading as calling home every day. It won’t always be earth-shaking news, but hearing that familiar voice every day settles your heart, and your own way of speaking becomes more and more like his.
920: let our words bear the fruit of the Spirit

Let our words bear the Spirit’s fruit of love, kindness and gentleness. (920 is our shorthand for living out the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.) The tone of voice we use at home, the words we type in group chats, the way we respond in meetings: all of these are places to bear fruit. Sometimes one gentle sentence opens a person’s heart more than ten correct ones.
Let’s do a little exercise. Think back: who did you say your last sentence to yesterday? What did you say? Did it draw that person’s heart a little closer, or push it a step away?
Multiplication: passing the gospel on to the next person

Language is a bridge between hearts, and also a bridge for the gospel. You came to know Jesus because of something someone said to you; now it’s your turn to use your words to pass the gospel on to the next person.
And you don’t need to be a great speaker. You don’t have to memorize a complete script; just honestly share, “This is how Jesus changed me.” A genuine testimony is often the strongest bridge of all.

This week’s action: every day this week, use one specific sentence to affirm or bless someone, such as a family member, a coworker, or a brother or sister in your fellowship. Remember to be specific: not “You’re great,” but “Thank you for pitching in to help me clean up yesterday; it really touched me.”

Brothers and sisters, limited words, unlimited meaning; through language one heart travels into another. Science tells us human language has a unique capacity for unlimited combination, and its origin remains a great mystery. The Bible tells us that in the beginning was the Word, that the speaking God made speaking humans in his image, and that the Word himself became flesh and came among us.
Please read John 1:14 again slowly in your heart. The Word who created language came in person among us to speak to us.
And ask yourself: Lately, have my words been building people up or tearing them down?
Let us pray together: Word made flesh, thank you for coming in person to speak to me. Cleanse my lips, so that my words carry grace and truth and become a blessing to others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. What new appreciation for the wonder of human language do the “LEGO bricks” and “Russian nesting dolls” analogies give you?
2. God let Adam name the animals, and Jesus is “the Word made flesh.” How do these two things shape the way you see every word you speak?
3. Whom do you plan to bless with one specific sentence this week? Also share a time when someone’s words deeply blessed you.
Made for Love: The Cloth Mother and the Triune God
We love him, because he first loved us. (1 John 4:19)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! If I asked you right now, “What does it take for a person to live a healthy, happy life?” you might say: money, a good job, a nutritious diet, plenty of exercise.

All of those make sense. But I want to tell you about a very special study. Since 1938, Harvard University has followed a group of people across their whole lives; it is one of the longest studies of adult development ever conducted. It followed them from youth into old age, looking at their work, marriages, health and happiness.
The study’s current director, Robert Waldinger, sums it up in one sentence: one of the keys to health and happiness is warm, good relationships.
Not wealth, not fame, but this: having people who love you, and loving them in return.

We can ask ourselves: if you came to the last day of your life and looked back, what would you most want to see one more time: the number in your bank account, or the faces of the people who love you?
Friends, God actually said this at the very beginning.
Yahweh God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.” (Genesis 2:18)
1. The story of the cloth mother
The milk bottle and the embrace

In 1958 the psychologist Harry Harlow carried out an experiment. He gave a group of baby monkeys a choice between two “surrogate mothers.” One was made of wire, cold and hard, but with a milk bottle attached. The other was wrapped in soft cloth, soft and warm, but with no milk.
Have a guess: which one did the baby monkeys choose?

By the logic of “follow whoever feeds you,” they should have chosen the wire mother, right? It was exactly the opposite. The baby monkeys spent most of their time clinging to the cloth mother, going over to the wire mother only when they were hungry to take a few sips of milk, and then hurrying back into the cloth mother’s arms.
This tells us that contact comfort attracted the baby monkeys more than food did. Life needs not only to be fed, but to be held.

It makes me think of many families. The parents work terribly hard, earning every dollar they can; the fridge is packed full, and there is one tutoring class after another. The children lack nothing, except a hug, except a grown-up willing to sit down and listen to them.

Friends, haven’t we sometimes accidentally become a “wire mother” or a “wire father”? We provide everything, but not the warmth. What children want is often not more milk bottles, but more soft cloth.

Maybe when you get home today, instead of first asking, “Have you finished your homework?” you could first ask, “How was your day?” and then quietly listen. That one question is a piece of soft cloth.
Let’s use an analogy. A glowing coal left in the fire keeps giving off heat and light. But pull it out on its own and set it aside, and before long it goes cold and black.

People are like that. Cut off from loving relationships, the heart slowly grows cold. Some people look fine on the outside, working hard and hitting their targets, but when they get home their hearts are cold, because they are a coal pulled out of the fire.
What this means for us spiritually

God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone.” Notice that this was said before humanity had sinned. In the Garden of Eden everything was perfect; only one thing was “not good”: the man was alone.
Brothers and sisters, needing relationships is not weakness; it is God’s design for humanity. Needing people doesn’t mean you aren’t spiritual enough; it shows that you were made in God’s image.
Some people are embarrassed to say, “I need you to be with me,” as if saying it were shameful. In fact, being willing to admit need is the beginning of humility; God made us to support one another.

The British psychiatrist John Bowlby proposed “attachment theory”: children need a stable emotional bond with their caregivers. It’s like a young tree that needs roots; when the roots are firm, the tree grows well.

Later Mary Ainsworth designed an observation method called the “Strange Situation.” She observed how young children respond when separated from and reunited with a caregiver, and identified secure and insecure patterns of attachment.

Here I want to say something especially comforting. Research also reminds us that early attachment patterns are linked to later relationships, but scholars still debate how large the effect is and whether it can change. Attachment is not fixed for life.

It’s like a tree bent by the wind when it was young: move it to good soil, give it a stake to lean on, and it can still slowly grow straight. The fellowship of the church is the good soil and the support that God has prepared for us.
So if you feel you were not loved well as a child, please don’t despair. Your story isn’t finished. In God’s family, in the love of brothers and sisters, a heart can be warmed again.

In 2010 a meta-analysis combined 148 studies with a total of 308,849 participants. It found that people with stronger social relationships had about a 50% greater likelihood of survival over the follow-up period.

Friends, that is a striking number. But we must also say honestly that this is correlational research; it cannot directly prove cause and effect, and the mechanisms are still being studied. Still, it clearly shows that relationships and health are closely linked.
In other words, coming to small group on the weekend and sharing meals and conversation with brothers and sisters may be good not only for your soul but quite possibly for your body too.

Of course, I’m not saying that coming to church guarantees you’ll live to a hundred; the research doesn’t say that, and neither do we. But at least we can confidently say this: God designed people to live in relationships, and living according to the design always works better. It’s like a car maintained according to the owner’s manual: it always runs more smoothly.
We love him, because he first loved us. (1 John 4:19)
What this means for us spiritually

Why do people need love so much? John says, “We love him, because he first loved us.” Love does not begin with us. We are like the moon: it gives off no light of its own; only because the sun shines on it first can it reflect light.
Only someone who has first been loved by God has an unending supply of love to love others.

So if you feel worn out from loving, unable to keep loving, perhaps it’s not that you haven’t tried hard enough, but that you have drifted too far from the sun. Come back to God and let his love shine on you again, and you will have light to reflect once more.
3. The triune God: an eternal fellowship of love
Let’s go back to Genesis. When God made human beings, he said something very special.
God said, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness …” (Genesis 1:26)

God says “let us” make man in “our” image. Christians believe that the one God exists in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Before the world was made, love was already flowing within God.
The Lord Jesus spoke this eternal secret in his prayer too:
… for you loved me before the foundation of the world. (John 17:24)
God did not create us because he was lonely
Think about it: if God were a solitary god, he would need to make creatures first in order to love. Like someone who lives alone and gets so lonely that he gets a puppy for company.

But the triune God is not like that. Before the foundation of the world, the Father loved the Son, the Son loved the Father, and the Holy Spirit was in their midst; love was already flowing within God like a river that never stops. God did not make us because he lacked something, but because his love was so abundant that it overflowed, and he invited us into that love.
So “God is love” is not a slogan. A solitary god would need creatures in order to love; but the triune God has always been love from eternity.

It’s like a warm family: the father and mother love each other, and the children feel surrounded by love at home. One day they decide to adopt a child, not because the house feels empty, but because there is so much love in the family that they want to share it. God inviting us to become his children is love like that.
God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him. (1 John 4:16)
What this means for us spiritually

We can reasonably infer that our deep need for love and relationship fits exactly with the Bible’s revelation. We are made in the image of the triune God, so we are made for relationship by nature. This is a theological and philosophical inference, but it explains the deepest longing of our hearts with perfect clarity.
We long for love because we are made in his image.
The order of relationships: God, self, others, tasks

Relationships have an order: God, self, others, tasks. Draw near to God first, and then you can love others in a healthy way. This is what we mean by “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” Many people turn the order upside down: they throw themselves into ministry first, and their relationships go cold and their spiritual life dries up. Like that coal, just when it is burning brightest, it leaves the fire.
Here’s a simple check: where did you spend the most time this week? Whose messages do you think of replying to first? Those two answers often reveal, very honestly, the order in our hearts.
235: don’t walk the road of faith alone

We need spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, and comrades in arms. (235 is our shorthand for these kinds of spiritual relationships.) Faith has never been a solo event; it is a team. A coal has to stay in the fire to keep burning. Ask yourself: Who are my spiritual companions? Who are my spiritual parents? Whom am I walking alongside?

It’s like climbing a mountain. Climb alone, and when you’re tired you want to give up. Climb with a group, with someone leading the way in front, someone giving you a push from behind, and someone beside you saying, “Keep going, we’re almost there,” and before you know it you’ve reached the top. The spiritual road is the same.

In the middle of busyness, stop first and see the person. A meeting can start five minutes late, but the weariness on a coworker’s face shouldn’t go unnoticed for five minutes. Your child’s homework can be checked a bit later, but the thing your child wants to tell you may have only this one chance tonight.
This week’s action: arrange to meet or call a friend or family member you haven’t been in touch with for a while, and give them your full attention, without looking at your phone.
Putting the phone down isn’t easy. You can put it in your bag, or turn it face down on the table. The other person will feel, “Right now, I matter to you.” That is the warmth of the cloth mother.

Brothers and sisters, the baby monkeys chose the cloth mother; the Harvard study says relationships make people healthy and happy; the meta-analysis shows relationships are linked to survival. All of this tells us that human beings are made for love.
And the Bible tells us why: because the God who made us is himself a fellowship of love.
Now please think of someone who once loved you unconditionally, and thank God for them. That love was a reflection of God’s love.
And honestly ask yourself: Lately, have I treated tasks as more important than people, and things as more important than relationships?

Let us pray together: Triune God, you are love, and you made me in your image. Fill me with your love, so that I first draw near to you and can then sincerely love the people around me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
